title: Folio 1: The Vizier on the Gallows
description: Ghazni, a thousand years ago. Sultan Mahmud is dead, his son Masud takes the throne, and the old vizier Hasanak is about to pay for one careless sentence. Beyhaqi, a young secretary at court, saw it all, and wrote it down years later in one of the most famous passages of Persian prose. A story about pride, revenge, a mother's dignity, and a historian who refused to lie.
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi, the account of Hasanak's execution (Balkh, 422 AH / 1032 CE)

title: Folio 2: Two Brothers, One Throne
description: In the spring of 1030, the great Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni dies, and his empire is left to the wrong son. His elder son Masud is far away in Isfahan, and his younger son Muhammad is already on the throne. Over six tense months, letters fly, armies change sides, and a kingmaker learns the price of making kings. Beyhaqi, who knew these men, tells us how it really went.
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi, the surviving part of volume five: the letter from Tiginabad, the arrest of Hajib Ali in Herat, and Masud's arrival in Balkh (421 AH / 1030 CE)

title: Folio 3: The Blind King Who Ruled Twice
description: A Sultan who reigned for five months is locked in a fortress by his own brother, and the world forgets him. Ten years later, a mutinous army drags him out and crowns him again. This is the strange fate of Amir Muhammad, son of Mahmud of Ghazni, and of the brother who took his throne.
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi (Muhammad in the fortress after Tiginabad, 421 AH / 1030 CE; Masud's departure for India after Dandanqan, 431-432 AH / 1040 CE), with the later chroniclers for the mutiny at Marikala, Masud's death at Giri and Mawdud's victory near Nangarhar (432 AH / 1041 CE)

title: Folio 4: The Judge Who Lied to Save a Life
description: A man sits blindfolded on the executioner's mat, and the sword is already drawn. In the middle of the night, the chief judge of the Abbasid empire rides to stop it, armed with nothing but words. This is the story of Afshin, Bu Dulaf and Ahmad ibn Abi Duwad, as Beyhaqi tells it.
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi, the story of Afshin and the deliverance of Bu Dulaf (told before the hanging of Hasanak, after Ismail ibn Shihab from Ahmad ibn Abi Duwad); with standard scholarship for Afshin's background and his trial and death (840-841 CE)

title: Folio 5: The Secretary Who Kept the Sultan's Secrets
description: On the day his friend was hanged, he refused to eat. On the night the empire began to crack, the sultan called him in alone. This is Bu Nasr Moshkan, master of the Ghaznavid chancery, Beyhaqi's teacher for nineteen years, and the quiet man who taught him how to survive a dangerous court and how to tell the truth about it.
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi: Bu Nasr's advice to Amir Masud (remnant of volume five); the hanging of Hasanak (volume six); Bu Nasr's counsel to the Amir, his offence at the Amir, and his death (volume nine, year 431 AH); with Encyclopaedia Iranica (Yusofi, 'Bayhaqi, Abu'l-Fazl') and standard reference works for dates (head of the chancery about 1011/12 to his death in 1039/40)

title: Folio 6: The Sultan and the Lion
description: Sick with fever, his club missed and his spear snapped, a young prince faced a wounded lion with nothing but his hands. Beyhaqi saw Masud of Ghazni hunt lions alone, stand barefoot in the snow, and kill eight lions in a day. But what does a lion hunt tell us about a king who would soon face enemies no spear could stop?
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi, volume six: the portrait of Amir Masud's habits and hunting (section on lion hunting: his training, winter hunts, the lion near Kikanan on the road to Multan, the elephant hunt in India, eight lions in one day near Herat, Bu Sahl Zawzani's Arabic verses), read in the Persian text (Ganjoor, Fayyaz edition p. 143); background from Encyclopaedia Iranica and Wikipedia ('Mas'ud I of Ghazni', 'Bahram V')

title: Folio 7: The Secret Order Against the Loyal General
description: His sultan signed a secret order to have him killed. The plot failed, and old Altuntash, governor of Khwarazm, had every reason to rebel. Instead he marched to war for the man who had tried to murder him. Beyhaqi's story of loyalty, a whispering courtier, and a death near Bukhara.
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi, volume seven: the sections on Bu Sahl's intrigue against Altuntash, the killing of Qaid Malanjuq, Amir Masud's letter to Altuntash, the planning of the war with Ali Tegin, and the choice of Khwaja Ahmad Abd al-Samad as vizier (423 AH / 1032 CE); volume nine for the vizier's remark; background from Encyclopaedia Iranica and Wikipedia ('Altuntash (khwarazmshah)', 'Abu Sahl Zawzani', 'Ahmad Shirazi')

title: Folio 8: The Nomads Who Asked for a Little Land
description: They came out of the desert with their tents and their herds, and they asked the sultan for a few dry pastures. Within three years they were sitting on his throne in Nishapur. This is how the Seljuqs, a small band of Turkmen nomads, arrived at the edge of the Ghaznavid empire, and how a proud sultan failed to take them seriously.
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi, the volumes on the years 426 to 429 AH (1035 to 1038 CE): the Seljuq letters to the court, the defeat of the chamberlain Begtoghdi near Nasa, the grant of Nasa, Farawa and Dihistan, Amir Masud's vow to take Hansi and his ministers' objections, and the loss of Nishapur; Beyhaqi's statement of method in the same work; background from Encyclopaedia Iranica, Britannica and Wikipedia ('Arslan Isra'il', 'Tughril I', 'Chaghri Beg', 'Begtoghdi', 'Battle of Nasa (1035)', 'Mas'ud I of Ghazni')
